item.title: Data Flow From API to UI: The Parts That Actually Break
item.description:
Drawing the layers for API-to-UI data flow is the part everyone can do: networking fetches, a view model holds state, the view renders. Boxes and arrows, done in an interview in two minutes. That diagram is also where the real problems are not. The hard parts of data flow are the ones the diagram hides, and they are where shipping apps actually break.

Here is a snippet close to what a lot of view models really contain. It looks reasonable. It has a bug that ships to production constantly.

item.title: The Architecture That Survives a Team Scaling From 5 to 20
item.description: When a team is five people, architecture is a technical question. When it is twenty, it is mostly an organizational one, and the codebase will end up shaped like the org chart whether you plan for it or not. That last part is Conway’s law, and on a growing iOS team it stops being a fun aphorism and starts being the thing that decides whether your release train runs on time.

item.title: The Shared Module Trap in iOS Apps
item.description:
Splitting an app into feature modules is the easy half and most teams get it roughly right. The half that quietly sinks the whole effort is the shared module: the Core, Common, or Shared target that everything else depends on. It starts as obvious good sense (“don’t duplicate networking”) and ends as a second monolith wearing a module’s clothes.

This is worth its own discussion because the shared module fails in specific, predictable ways, and once you can name them you can design around them.

item.title: Monolith vs Modular iOS: What Modularization Actually Costs
item.description:
“Should we modularize the app?” gets argued like a values question, monolith for the scrappy, modules for the grown-ups. It is not a values question. Modularization buys specific things and costs specific things, both measurable, and the teams that get burned are the ones that paid the cost without checking whether they needed what it bought.

Let’s price it out properly, because the usual pros-and-cons list (“easier to scale”, “more complex setup”) is too vague to make a decision with.

item.title: Why UIKit Pushes You Into a Massive View Controller
item.description:
Every iOS team eventually fights the same file. A view controller that started small and is now four figures of line count, the one nobody volunteers to touch. The usual explanation is discipline: someone got lazy, nobody refactored. That explanation is comfortable and mostly wrong.

Massive View Controller is not a discipline failure. It is what UIKit’s design pushes you toward by default. If you understand the mechanism, you stop fighting symptoms and start removing the actual causes. So let’s look at why the controller becomes a magnet, and then at what each escape hatch genuinely costs, because none of them are free.
